title: Developer-friendly status brief and replay choices
summary: Compact customer-facing brief explaining a short-lived KV cache corruption that caused intermittent mis-ordered streaming chunks and elevated latency for chat and streaming endpoints in the eu-west region. This doc is written for technical customers (developer and platform teams) and outlines the public status update language, a concise postmortem summary, recommended verification/replay options, and minimal steps customers can take to validate their data integrity.
status_update_snippet: At 2026-03-25T02:10Z we detected an increase in streaming session reorders and latency for requests routed to eu-west. We applied a staged rollback of a runtime cache change at 02:32Z and fully restored normal behaviour by 02:46Z. No tenant data was exfiltrated; some in-flight responses were duplicated or arrived out-of-order for ~36 minutes. We are continuing a technical review and will publish a post-incident verification package.
customer_impact: Customers using chat/streaming APIs in eu-west may have seen responses arrive in the wrong order, duplicated output tokens, or transient delays. Synchronous generation calls (non-streaming) were largely unaffected. The issue impacted ~0.7% of requests in the region during the window. Customers with strict sequence expectations or downstream dedup logic should validate replay choices below.
root_cause_summary: A recent optimization to the KV cache eviction path introduced a race when the runtime attempted concurrent prefix repairs during heavy prefix-sharing workloads. In a narrow timing window, the cache returned stale KV chunks that resulted in misapplied token order during streaming assembly. The change passed unit and integration tests but did not exercise the observed prefix-concurrency pattern.
what_we_did:
- Immediately rolled back the KV-prefetch optimization to the prior safe behavior (02:32Z).
- Triggered targeted cache flush across affected eu-west nodes and monitored for reorders.
- Deployed a small instrumentation patch to increase visibility into cache-hit/miss timing and ordering.
- Opened an ongoing root cause investigation and added a regression test exercising the high-concurrency prefix pattern.
timeline: 2026-03-25T02:10Z — Monitoring alert: elevated streaming reorders and latency in eu-west
2026-03-25T02:17Z — Engineering on-call begins investigation; replicated mis-order locally with curated workload
2026-03-25T02:32Z — Rollback of KV-prefetch optimization initiated across eu-west pool
2026-03-25T02:37Z — Partial recovery observed (reorders dropping), mitigation follow-up: targeted cache flush
2026-03-25T02:46Z — Full recovery observed, normal traffic metrics resumed
2026-03-25T03:10Z — Post-recovery monitoring: 30m watch period started, no recurrence detected
postmortem_high_level: This was an availability/regression incident caused by a runtime optimization that did not account for a high-concurrency cache prefix pattern. The primary fix is two-fold: revert the optimization (already done for immediate safety) and ship a corrected implementation with explicit concurrency control and unit/integration coverage before re-enabling. We will also add a directed chaos test to the nightly suite to exercise prefix sharing under load.
recommended_customer_verification_and_re:
1) If you observed out-of-order streaming responses and need deterministic ordering, consider replaying impacted requests using the request timestamps in your logs and our replay endpoint (see evidence package).
2) For clients that are tolerant of duplicates, apply idempotency or simple dedup on token hashes for the short window (approx 02:10–02:46Z).
3) If you need assistance deciding whether to replay, open a support ticket with request_ids and timestamps; our incident team will evaluate the evidence bundle and advise a targeted replay.
4) We are offering a proof bundle (see links) that contains hashed request/response pairs for tenant verification without exposing raw payloads.
customer_facing_faq: Q: Did this expose customer data? A: No. The issue affected in-memory cache ordering; there was no exfiltration to third parties and persistent storage was not involved.
Q: Will you bill for replayed requests? A: We are not charging customers for replays triggered specifically to remediate this incident. Please mention INC-2381 in the support ticket.

Q: How can I prevent this on my side? A: Add idempotency and sequence checks in the client where ordering is important. We will also provide an SDK patch with optional stricter client-side reassembly helpers within two weeks.
Q: Will the optimization be reintroduced? A: Yes, but only after a corrected implementation, more thorough concurrency tests, and a phased canary roll with stronger telemetry.

contacts: For support and tailored replay help open a ticket at support@redwood.ai with subject 'INC-2381 replay help' or contact your CSM. For technical liaison: on-call engineering Slack #inc-2381-runtime-kv-cache. Postmortem will be published to Confluence when internal RCA completes.
notes_to_ops: Keep an eye on metrics: streaming.reorder_rate, stream.latency.p95, cache.prefix_concurrency_index. If reorder spikes above 0.25% baseline, throttle new KV-prefetch-enabled canaries and escalate to runtime lead.
endnote: We know ordering and streaming semantics are crucial for many developer workflows. Our immediate priority was to restore correct behavior; next priority is to prevent recurrence with improved tests and safer rollout gates. We will share a follow-up with the corrected implementation timeline and the public postmortem link.
